disclaimer: ABF is an audit workbench. Screening conclusions are indicative and cite the rule applied. They are not legal advice, a conformity assessment, or a certification decision. ISO/IEC 42001 control bodies are titles only; obtain the standard for authentic text. Where ABF authors a procedure or evidence list, it is labeled as such.

sources.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0
sources.license_note: U.S. government work; public domain. AI RMF is voluntary and use-case agnostic.

sources.name: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
sources.license_note: EU legislative text is public. Application dates are staggered (Art. 113).

sources.name: ISO/IEC 42001:2023 — AI management system
sources.license_note: Control titles only. Official 'shall' statements are copyright ISO and are not reproduced. Use the purchased standard (and Annex B guidance) for implementation and certification.

sources.name: SR 11-7 / OCC Bulletin 2011-12 — Supervisory Guidance on Model Risk Management
sources.license_note: U.S. federal supervisory guidance. Applies to banking organizations supervised by the OCC, Federal Reserve, and FDIC; not automatically to every AI system.

sources.name: OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications 2025
sources.license_note: OWASP materials are typically CC BY-SA. Entries are threat categories, not regulatory controls.

sources.name: NIST AI 600-1 — Generative AI Profile
sources.license_note: U.S. government work. Profile is voluntary. Lists 12 GAI risks and suggested actions mapped to AI RMF subcategories.

procedure.title: Legal and regulatory inventory for the in-scope AI system
procedure.inquiry: Walk me through the inventory of laws, regulations, and internal policies you have mapped to this system, including who owns updates when the intended purpose changes.
procedure.observe: Inspect the mapping register (or equivalent) for this system. Confirm it names concrete instruments (e.g., EU AI Act articles, SR 11-7 if a bank model, privacy law) rather than a generic 'AI policy' bullet. Check last-review date against a material change (new use case, new model provider, new geography).
evidence: AI system legal/regulatory mapping register with owners and review dates
Intended-purpose statement used as the mapping input
Change-management ticket showing the mapping was revisited after a material change
procedure.test: Select the in-scope system. Agree intended purpose with the owner. Independently list candidate instruments from the ABF screening. Compare to the auditee's register and document gaps. Do not treat an uncited 'AI ethics policy' as coverage of a named article.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

procedure.title: AI system inventory completeness
procedure.inquiry: How do new LLM apps, copilots, and vendor embeddings enter the AI inventory, and what is excluded by policy?
procedure.observe: Compare the official inventory to shadow sources: SaaS spend, API keys, vector databases, and MLflow/model-registry entries. Look for unregistered RAG or agent prototypes in production paths.
evidence: Current AI / model inventory extract with owner, intended purpose, and risk tier
Procedure for adding, changing, and decommissioning inventory records
Reconciliation sample against cloud billing or API-key inventory
procedure.test: Sample five production AI uses from a non-inventory source; trace each to an inventory record or document an exception.

procedure.title: Human-AI configuration and oversight roles
procedure.inquiry: Who is allowed to accept, override, or halt this system's output, and what competence is required of that person?
procedure.observe: Review RACI / job descriptions for oversight. In a live walkthrough, ask the operator to show the override or stop path. If none exists, document residual automation-bias risk.
evidence: Documented human-oversight procedure (roles, training, escalation)
Screenshot or demo of override / stop control in the production UI or API
Training or competency records for persons assigned oversight
procedure.test: Trace one production decision path from model output to human action. Confirm the assigned person can interrupt the system.

procedure.title: Third-party model, data, and tool due diligence
procedure.inquiry: What residual rights does the vendor have over prompts, embeddings, and logs, and how was that verified in the contract and DPA?
procedure.observe: Read the enterprise agreement and data-processing terms for training-use, sub-processors, residency, and audit rights. Confirm the running environment matches the contracted tier (e.g., enterprise vs consumer API).
evidence: Executed enterprise agreement / DPA with model or vector-DB vendor
Vendor due-diligence file (SOC 2, ISO 27001, model card, data-use representations)
Configuration evidence that production traffic uses the contracted endpoint/tier
procedure.test: For the production endpoint, compare contract, key/tenant configuration, and a sample request log.

Deployment topology (regions, tenants, connected tools)

procedure.title: Task and method characterization
procedure.inquiry: Which tasks are classification, generation, retrieval, ranking, or tool-calling, and which model or component performs each?
procedure.observe: Walk the runtime graph (orchestrator, retriever, tools). Identify where untrusted content enters the prompt.

Model and component inventory (base model, fine-tunes, retrievers, tools)
Description of human vs automated task split

procedure.title: Documented human-oversight process
procedure.inquiry: In what cases must a human review output before it takes effect, and how is that enforced technically rather than by policy alone?
procedure.observe: Attempt (or review a recorded test of) a path that should require approval. Confirm the tool cannot complete without the approval token.
evidence: Oversight design (human-in-the-loop vs human-on-the-loop vs human-in-command)
Enforcement mechanism (workflow, allowlist, dual control)
Exception log for skipped reviews
procedure.test: Select one high-impact action. Verify a control prevents unattended execution.

procedure.title: Validity, reliability, and documented limits
procedure.inquiry: What held-out or production-like evaluation shows the system is valid for the stated purpose, and where do you tell operators it does not generalize?
procedure.observe: Review eval sets for leakage from training. For generative systems, inspect groundedness / hallucination metrics against the retrieval corpus, not only chatbot preference scores.
evidence: Evaluation report with datasets, metrics, dates, and owners
Documented known failure modes and operating limits
Sign-off that residual error is within risk tolerance
procedure.test: Re-perform or inspect a sample of evaluation cases. Confirm metrics match the intended purpose (e.g., credit default vs BLEU).
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

procedure.title: Security and resilience evaluation
procedure.inquiry: Which adversarial tests (prompt injection, data exfiltration, tool abuse) were run against this build, and who triaged the results?
procedure.observe: Review red-team or eval-harness output. Confirm findings were closed or risk-accepted with an owner.
evidence: Security test plan and results for the current production version
Guardrail / filter configuration (input and output)
Incident or bug tickets from failed adversarial tests
procedure.test: Map tests to OWASP LLM Top 10 2025 entries that apply to this architecture. Identify untested categories.

procedure.title: Privacy risk of prompts, logs, and retrieval
procedure.inquiry: Where do prompts, completions, embeddings, and evaluator traces live, for how long, and who can replay them?
procedure.observe: Inspect log stores, vendor training-use settings, and retention jobs. Confirm production is not on a consumer endpoint that reserves training rights.
evidence: Data-flow diagram for prompts, embeddings, logs, and fine-tune sets
Retention / TTL configuration and access-control lists
Vendor data-use setting evidence (enterprise opt-out / no-training)
procedure.test: Trace one customer utterance from UI to storage. Confirm deletion/TTL and access on a sample record.

procedure.title: Fairness and bias evaluation
procedure.inquiry: For this intended purpose, which groups did you test, which metrics, and what threshold would block release?
procedure.observe: Do not accept a generic 'we use a fair model' statement. Require slice metrics or a documented reason that quantitative fairness measurement is not applicable, per MEASURE 1.1 (unmeasured characteristics must be documented).
evidence: Bias / fairness test report tied to the intended purpose
Definition of protected or sensitive attributes used (or legal basis for not processing them)
Mitigations and residual-risk acceptance
procedure.test: If Annex III employment, credit, or education applies, treat this as a key control. Sample whether production monitoring continues slice metrics.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

procedure.title: Disengage, override, and deactivation
procedure.inquiry: Show me how you disable this system or a single tenant within an agreed time, including revoke of model API keys and agent tool credentials.
procedure.observe: Table-top or live kill-switch. Confirm it covers orchestrator, tools, and scheduled jobs, not only the chat UI.
evidence: Documented deactivation / rollback procedure with RTO
Evidence of a tested disable (ticket, game-day, or change record)
Key and credential revocation path (IdP, API gateway)
procedure.test: Inspect last test of deactivation. If never tested, raise as a design gap against MANAGE 2.4 and, if high-risk, EU Art. 14 stop-button language.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

procedure.title: Monitoring of pre-trained and vendor models
procedure.inquiry: How do you learn that the vendor changed the model, the system prompt, or the safety layer under your deployment?
procedure.observe: Check for pinned model versions vs floating 'latest'. Review changelog subscription and regression evals on vendor updates.
evidence: Pinned model version IDs in production config
Vendor change-notification process
Regression evaluation after the last vendor update
procedure.test: Compare production model identifier to the last approved version in change control.

obligations.title: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.
obligations.official_text: Post-deployment AI system monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users and other relevant AI actors, appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response, recovery, and change management.

procedure.title: Post-deployment monitoring, appeals, and incidents
procedure.inquiry: Where do users contest an output, and how does that feed evaluation and incident response?
procedure.observe: Follow one complaint or override into the monitoring backlog. Confirm drift, toxicity, and tool-error metrics exist for genAI, not only classic ML PSI.
evidence: Post-deployment monitoring plan and dashboards
User appeal / feedback channel
Incident response playbook covering AI-specific events
procedure.test: Sample two production incidents or complaints and trace to a logged event and a documented response.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Measurable activities for continual improvements are integrated into AI system updates and include regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.
obligations.official_text: Measurable activities for continual improvements are integrated into AI system updates and include regular engagement with interested parties, including relevant AI actors.

obligations.title: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities. Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors are followed and documented.
obligations.official_text: Incidents and errors are communicated to relevant AI actors, including affected communities. Processes for tracking, responding to, and recovering from incidents and errors are followed and documented.

obligations.title: Prohibited AI practices
obligations.official_text: Places on the Union market, puts into service, or uses of listed practices are prohibited. The list includes (among others) subliminal/manipulative techniques causing or reasonably likely to cause significant harm; exploiting vulnerabilities of age, disability or socio-economic circumstances; social scoring causing detrimental treatment; untargeted scraping of facial images to build/expand facial-recognition databases; emotion recognition in the workplace or educational institutions (with limited medical/safety exceptions); biometric categorisation inferring certain sensitive attributes; assessing criminality solely on profiling or personality traits; and real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement except narrowly defined cases. Consult the authentic Article 5 text for exceptions and conditions.

obligations.title: Classification rules for high-risk AI systems
obligations.official_text: An AI system is high-risk if (Art. 6(1)) it is a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by Union harmonisation legislation in Annex I and is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that legislation; or (Art. 6(2)) it is listed in Annex III. Art. 6(3) provides that Annex III systems are not high-risk if they do not pose a significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights, including by not materially influencing the outcome of decision making. The exception does not apply if the system profiles natural persons. Providers that conclude an Annex III system is not high-risk must document that assessment before placing the system on the market or putting it into service.

obligations.title: Risk management system
obligations.official_text: A continuous, iterative risk-management system shall be established, implemented, documented and maintained throughout the lifecycle of a high-risk AI system: identification and analysis of known and reasonably foreseeable risks; estimation and evaluation of risks arising from intended purpose and reasonably foreseeable misuse; evaluation of risks from post-market monitoring data; and adoption of appropriate and targeted risk-management measures.

procedure.title: High-risk risk-management system (Art. 9)
procedure.inquiry: Show the living Art. 9 file for this system: foreseeable misuse, residual risk, and measures tied to post-market data.
procedure.observe: The file should be iterative (versions), not a one-time DPIA copy-paste. Check reasonably foreseeable misuse (jailbreak, over-reliance, wrong population).
evidence: Risk-management system documentation for the system lifecycle
Register of known and reasonably foreseeable risks
Link from post-market monitoring data into risk updates
procedure.test: Pick one residual risk. Trace identification → measure → owner → residual rating → monitoring metric.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Data and data governance
obligations.official_text: Training, validation and testing data sets shall be subject to appropriate data-governance and management practices. Data sets shall be relevant, sufficiently representative, and to the best extent possible, free of errors and complete in view of the intended purpose. Appropriate statistical properties, examination of possible biases, and relevant data-protection measures shall be considered.

procedure.title: Training, validation, and test data governance (Art. 10)
procedure.inquiry: For each training/validation/test set: origin, representativeness versus intended purpose, known gaps, and bias examination.
procedure.observe: If the team only uses a third-party foundation model, Art. 10 still matters for fine-tunes, RAG corpora, and evaluator sets the provider controls.
evidence: Dataset inventory with intended-purpose alignment notes
Bias/quality examination records
Data-protection measures for personal data in those sets
procedure.test: Sample one dataset. Confirm documented provenance and a quality/bias check dated before the last training or index build.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Technical documentation
obligations.official_text: Technical documentation shall be drawn up before the high-risk AI system is placed on the market or put into service and shall be kept up to date. It shall demonstrate compliance with Section 2 and provide national competent authorities and notified bodies with the information necessary to assess that compliance. Minimum content is set out in Annex IV.

procedure.title: Annex IV technical documentation
procedure.inquiry: Walk through the Annex IV pack: intended purpose, design specifications, data, TEVV, cybersecurity, and human oversight.
procedure.observe: Confirm the pack matches the running system version (commit, model ID, prompt version).
evidence: Technical documentation mapped to Annex IV headings
Version identifier that matches production
Instructions for use provided to deployers (Art. 13)
procedure.test: Tick Annex IV headings against the file. Record missing headings as exceptions. Do not invent content.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Record-keeping
obligations.official_text: High-risk AI systems shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system. Logging shall enable identification of situations that may result in the system presenting a risk or in a substantial modification, and shall facilitate post-market monitoring and operation monitoring.

obligations.title: Transparency and provision of information to deployers
obligations.official_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed so that their operation is sufficiently transparent to enable deployers to interpret a system's output and use it appropriately. Instructions for use shall include identity and contact of the provider, characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance, human-oversight measures, and the computational and hardware resources needed.

obligations.title: Human oversight
obligations.official_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use. Oversight measures shall enable the persons to whom human oversight is assigned to understand the capacities and limitations, remain aware of automation bias, correctly interpret output, decide not to use or to disregard/override the output, and intervene or interrupt the system through a stop button or similar procedure.

procedure.title: Human oversight operability (Art. 14)
procedure.inquiry: How does an overseer interpret output, ignore it, and interrupt the system? How do you reduce automation bias?
procedure.observe: Live demo of stop/override. Check whether the UI discloses confidence/limits or presents output as authoritative fact.
evidence: Oversight design in technical documentation
Deployer instructions describing oversight measures
Training material on automation bias for overseers
procedure.test: Execute (or review recording of) interrupt and override. Confirm logs capture the human action (Art. 12).
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity
obligations.official_text: High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed so that they achieve an appropriate level of accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity, and perform consistently in those respects throughout their lifecycle. Accuracy metrics shall be declared in the instructions for use. Resilience shall address errors, faults, inconsistencies, and attempts by unauthorised third parties to alter use or performance (including data poisoning and adversarial examples).

procedure.title: Accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity (Art. 15)
procedure.inquiry: Which accuracy metrics are declared to deployers, and which robustness tests cover data poisoning and adversarial inputs?
procedure.observe: Instructions for use should declare metrics (Art. 15). Compare declared metrics to actual eval reports.
evidence: Declared accuracy metrics in instructions for use
Robustness / adversarial evaluation results
Cybersecurity measures for the AI pipeline (incl. poisoning and adversarial examples)
procedure.test: Match declared metrics to the latest evaluation. Inspect one adversarial test case and its disposition.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Obligations of providers of high-risk AI systems
obligations.official_text: Providers shall ensure conformity with Section 2 requirements; indicate name/trademark and contact; have a quality management system (Art. 17); keep documentation (Art. 18); keep logs when under their control (Art. 19); take corrective actions (Art. 20); cooperate with competent authorities; demonstrate conformity on request; ensure accessibility requirements; and fulfil registration obligations (Art. 49).

obligations.title: Quality management system
obligations.official_text: Providers shall put a quality management system in place that documents strategy for regulatory compliance, design/examination/verification/validation procedures, data-management procedures, the risk-management system, post-market monitoring, serious-incident reporting, communication with authorities, and resource/accountability arrangements.

obligations.title: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems
obligations.official_text: Deployers shall take appropriate technical and organisational measures to use the system in accordance with the instructions for use; assign human oversight to persons with necessary competence, training and authority; ensure input data is relevant and sufficiently representative where they exercise control; monitor operation and report risks/serious incidents to the provider and authorities as required; keep logs under their control for a period of at least six months (subject to Union or national law); inform workers' representatives and affected workers; register use where they are public authorities or Union institutions; and inform natural persons subject to the use of certain Annex III systems that they are subject to that use (Art. 26(11)).

procedure.title: Deployer obligations walkthrough (Art. 26)
procedure.inquiry: Who is assigned oversight, how do you monitor operation against the instructions for use, and where are logs retained (at least six months if under your control)?
procedure.observe: For workplace systems, check worker information. For credit/insurance/public bodies, check FRIA (Art. 27) separately.
evidence: Record of assigned overseers and their competence
Operating procedure aligned to provider instructions for use
Log-retention configuration (≥ 6 months where Art. 26 applies and logs are under deployer control)
Worker notification evidence if used in the workplace
procedure.test: Sample log retention and one monitoring exception. Confirm reporting path to the provider for serious incidents.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment
obligations.official_text: Before deploying a high-risk system referred to in Art. 6(2), deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or private entities providing public services, shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights. The same duty applies to deployers of Annex III point 5(b) and 5(c) systems (creditworthiness of natural persons, and life/health insurance risk assessment and pricing). Annex III point 2 (critical infrastructure) is excluded from this FRIA duty.

procedure.title: Fundamental rights impact assessment (Art. 27)
procedure.inquiry: Was an Art. 27 FRIA required, who performed it, and how did it change deployment conditions?
procedure.observe: Confirm whether the deployer is a public body, a private provider of public services, or a deployer of Annex III 5(b)/(c). Critical infrastructure (Annex III(2)) is excluded from this FRIA duty.
evidence: FRIA document (or documented determination that Art. 27 does not apply)
Notification to the market surveillance authority where required
Mitigations feeding the deployer operating procedure
procedure.test: Check actor type and Annex III paragraph against Art. 27 scope. Do not demand a FRIA from in-scope-excluded deployers.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Transparency obligations for certain AI systems
obligations.official_text: Providers shall ensure that AI systems intended to interact directly with natural persons are designed so that the persons concerned are informed that they are interacting with an AI system (unless this is obvious from the point of view of a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person). Providers of AI systems generating synthetic audio, image, video or text content shall ensure the outputs are marked in a machine-readable format and detectable as artificially generated or manipulated. Deployers of emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems shall inform natural persons exposed thereto. Deployers of systems that generate or manipulate image, audio or video content constituting a deep fake shall disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated.

procedure.title: User-facing AI and synthetic-content disclosure
procedure.inquiry: How is a person told they are interacting with AI, and how is synthetic media marked in a machine-readable way?
procedure.observe: Chat UI, email agents, and generated PDFs. Check watermarking/manifests for media, not only a footer disclaimer.
evidence: UI/UX evidence of AI interaction notice
Technical marking of synthetic content (where Art. 50(2) applies)
Deep-fake or emotion-recognition disclosure procedure if those systems are in use
procedure.test: Use the system as a new user. Record whether the AI nature is disclosed before reliance on output.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Classification of GPAI models with systemic risk
obligations.official_text: A general-purpose AI model is classified as a GPAI model with systemic risk if it has high-impact capabilities evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks. A model is presumed to have high-impact capabilities when the cumulative amount of computation used for its training is greater than 10^25 FLOPs. Providers shall notify the Commission without delay and in any event within two weeks if the threshold is met.

obligations.title: Obligations for providers of GPAI models
obligations.official_text: Providers of general-purpose AI models shall draw up and keep up-to-date technical documentation, including the training and testing process and the results of its evaluation; draw up and keep up-to-date information and documentation for downstream providers; put in place a policy to comply with Union copyright law; and publish a sufficiently detailed summary about the content used for training. Certain free and open-source GPAI models that are not systemic-risk models have a reduced set of these obligations.

procedure.title: GPAI provider documentation and training-content summary
procedure.inquiry: Show the Art. 53 technical documentation, downstream-provider information, copyright policy, and public training-content summary.
procedure.observe: If claiming open-source reduced duties, test whether weights, architecture, and usage information are actually public and whether the model is systemic-risk.
evidence: GPAI technical documentation
Downstream information pack
Copyright-compliance policy
Published training-content summary
procedure.test: Tick Art. 53 items. If systemic-risk indicators exist, continue to Art. 55 procedures.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.title: Obligations of providers of GPAI models with systemic risk
obligations.official_text: In addition to Art. 53, providers of GPAI models with systemic risk shall perform model evaluation in accordance with standardised protocols and tools reflecting the state of the art, including conducting and documenting adversarial testing; assess and mitigate possible systemic risks; track, document and report serious incidents and possible corrective measures to the AI Office and national competent authorities without undue delay; and ensure an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure.

obligations.title: Technical documentation referred to in Article 11(1)
obligations.official_text: Annex IV specifies the minimum technical-documentation content for high-risk AI systems, including a general description of the system and intended purpose; a detailed description of the elements and development process (design specifications, design choices, data requirements, training/testing/validation procedures, cybersecurity measures); monitoring, functioning and control; the risk-management system; changes over the lifecycle; a list of harmonised standards applied; the EU declaration of conformity; and a description of the system in operation.

obligations.title: Biometrics (where permitted)
obligations.official_text: Remote biometric identification (excluding verification whose sole purpose is to confirm a person is who they claim to be); biometric categorisation according to sensitive or protected attributes; emotion recognition.

obligations.title: Critical infrastructure
obligations.official_text: AI systems intended to be used as safety components in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure, road traffic, or the supply of water, gas, heating or electricity.

obligations.title: Education and vocational training
obligations.official_text: Access/admission/assignment to education; evaluation of learning outcomes; assessing the appropriate level of education; monitoring/detecting prohibited student behaviour during tests.

obligations.title: Employment, workers' management and access to self-employment
obligations.official_text: Recruitment or selection (targeted job ads, analysing/filtering applications, evaluating candidates); decisions affecting terms of work, promotion or termination; allocating tasks based on behaviour or personal traits; monitoring and evaluating performance.

obligations.title: Essential private and public services and benefits
obligations.official_text: Public-authority evaluation of eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services (including healthcare); creditworthiness/credit scoring of natural persons except fraud detection; life and health insurance risk assessment and pricing; emergency-call classification, dispatch priority, and emergency patient triage.

obligations.title: Law enforcement (where permitted)
obligations.official_text: Assessing risk of becoming a crime victim; polygraphs; evaluating reliability of evidence; assessing risk of offending or re-offending (not solely on profiling as defined in Directive (EU) 2016/680); profiling in detection, investigation or prosecution of criminal offences.

obligations.title: Migration, asylum and border control management (where permitted)
obligations.official_text: Polygraphs; assessing security, irregular-migration, or health risk of a person entering a Member State; assisting examination of asylum, visa or residence applications; detecting, recognising or identifying persons except verification of travel documents.

obligations.title: Administration of justice and democratic processes
obligations.official_text: Assisting a judicial authority in researching/interpreting facts and the law and applying the law to facts, or similar use in alternative dispute resolution; influencing the outcome of an election or referendum or voting behaviour (excluding administrative/logistical campaign tools to which persons are not directly exposed).

obligations.citation: Board/OCC/FDIC SR 11-7 (OCC Bulletin 2011-12), Model development, implementation, and use
obligations.title: Model development, implementation, and use
obligations.official_text: Supervisory guidance expects sound development, implementation, and use of models: clear statement of purpose, conceptually sound design, appropriate data, testing before implementation, and use consistent with the model's design and documented limitations.

obligations.title: Model validation (independent)
obligations.official_text: Effective validation is performed by staff with appropriate incentives, competence, and influence, independent of model development and use. Core elements include evaluation of conceptual soundness (including developmental evidence), ongoing monitoring (including process verification and benchmarking), and outcomes analysis (including back-testing).

procedure.title: Independent model validation (SR 11-7)
procedure.inquiry: Who validated this model, how are they independent, and which of conceptual soundness, ongoing monitoring, and outcomes analysis are complete?
procedure.observe: Validator reporting line, last validation memo, limitations, and restrictions on use. Chatbots used as decision models still need a documented model definition.
evidence: Independent validation report
Model inventory record and risk tier
Ongoing monitoring / back-testing evidence
Limitations and restrictions communicated to users
procedure.test: Confirm independence (no developer self-validation as the sole line). Tick the three validation elements from SR 11-7.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.citation: Board/OCC/FDIC SR 11-7 (OCC Bulletin 2011-12), Governance, policies, and controls
obligations.title: Governance, policies, and controls
obligations.official_text: Board and senior management are expected to establish a model risk management framework with policies, procedures, staff, and controls commensurate with the bank's risk exposures, including a comprehensive model inventory, documentation standards, and limits on use of models that are deficient or that have identified weaknesses.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM01:Prompt Injection
obligations.title: Prompt Injection
obligations.official_text: User or untrusted content alters the LLM's behaviour or instructions (direct or indirect).

procedure.title: Prompt injection (direct and indirect)
procedure.inquiry: How do you separate untrusted retrieved or tool content from developer instructions, and what tests prove the boundary holds?
procedure.observe: Live prompt construction. Look for delimiters, privilege reduction, and tool-call confirmation. For RAG, inspect a document containing instruction-like text.
evidence: Prompt-template and orchestration code showing instruction/data separation
Adversarial test results for direct and indirect injection
Tool-gateway policy that does not blindly execute model-proposed actions
procedure.test: Review one indirect-injection test using retrieved content. Confirm the tool layer does not treat model text as authorization.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM02:Sensitive Information Disclosure
obligations.title: Sensitive Information Disclosure
obligations.official_text: The system reveals secrets, personal data, or proprietary content in outputs or side channels.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM03:Supply Chain
obligations.title: Supply Chain
obligations.official_text: Compromised models, datasets, plugins, or third-party components introduce risk into the LLM application.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM04:Data and Model Poisoning
obligations.title: Data and Model Poisoning
obligations.official_text: Training, fine-tuning, or embedding data is manipulated to degrade or steer model behaviour.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM05:Improper Output Handling
obligations.title: Improper Output Handling
obligations.official_text: Insufficient validation of model output leads to XSS, RCE, data exfiltration, or privilege issues downstream.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM06:Excessive Agency
obligations.title: Excessive Agency
obligations.official_text: The LLM is granted too much autonomy, functionality, or permission to invoke tools and take actions.

procedure.title: Excessive agency / tool authorization
procedure.inquiry: Which tools can the agent invoke, under whose identity, and what actions require step-up approval?
procedure.observe: Tool manifest (MCP or equivalent). Attempt a write action under a read-only user. Confirm identity propagation vs a shared superuser token.
evidence: Tool allowlist / schema with least privilege
End-user identity propagation design
Logs of blocked tool calls
procedure.test: Map each production tool to a business-justified permission. Fail if a general-purpose code-exec or payment tool is enabled without dual control.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM07:System Prompt Leakage
obligations.title: System Prompt Leakage
obligations.official_text: Hidden developer instructions, secrets, or policy text in the system prompt are extracted.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM08:Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
obligations.title: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
obligations.official_text: Retrieval/embedding pipelines allow data leakage, poisoning, or authorization bypass via the vector store.

procedure.title: Vector store authorization and poisoning
procedure.inquiry: Does retrieval enforce the requesting user's entitlements, and how is corpus integrity controlled?
procedure.observe: Query the index as a low-privilege user. Inspect ingestion pipeline for access control on source documents and for poisoning tests.
evidence: Document-level ACL enforcement at retrieval time (not only at UI)
Ingestion provenance and change control for the corpus
Tests for embedding inversion / cross-tenant retrieval if multi-tenant
procedure.test: Two-user retrieval test: user A must not receive user B documents. Record queries and hits.
procedure.authored_by: ABF workpaper procedure (not the source standard)

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM09:Misinformation
obligations.title: Misinformation
obligations.official_text: The system produces false, unsupported, or hallucinated content that users may rely on.

obligations.citation: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, LLM10:Unbounded Consumption
obligations.title: Unbounded Consumption
obligations.official_text: Uncontrolled inference, tool calls, or context growth causes denial of service or cost/resource abuse.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: CBRN information or capabilities
obligations.title: CBRN information or capabilities
obligations.official_text: Generative systems may lower barriers to chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear information or capabilities.

obligations.title: Confabulation
obligations.official_text: The model produces plausible but incorrect or fabricated content (hallucination).

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Dangerous or violent recommendations
obligations.title: Dangerous or violent recommendations
obligations.official_text: Outputs may recommend or enable dangerous or violent activity.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Data privacy
obligations.title: Data privacy
obligations.official_text: Training, prompts, retrieval, or outputs may expose or mishandle personal or sensitive data.

obligations.title: Environmental
obligations.official_text: Training and operating generative models can have significant energy and environmental impact.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Harmful bias and homogenization
obligations.title: Harmful bias and homogenization
obligations.official_text: Generated content may encode harmful bias or collapse diverse outputs toward homogenized representations.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Human-AI configuration
obligations.title: Human-AI configuration
obligations.official_text: Risks arise from how humans and generative systems are configured to interact, oversee, and rely on each other.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Information integrity
obligations.title: Information integrity
obligations.official_text: Generated or manipulated content can undermine authenticity, provenance, and public information integrity.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Information security
obligations.title: Information security
obligations.official_text: Generative systems expand attack surface (prompt injection, data exfiltration, malware generation, credential leakage).

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Intellectual property
obligations.title: Intellectual property
obligations.official_text: Training data and outputs may implicate copyright, trademark, trade secrets, or licensed content.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Obscene, degrading, and/or abusive content
obligations.title: Obscene, degrading, and/or abusive content
obligations.official_text: Systems may generate or fail to block obscene, degrading, or abusive material.

obligations.citation: NIST AI 600-1 (July 2024), GAI risk: Value chain and component integration
obligations.title: Value chain and component integration
obligations.official_text: Risk concentrates in third-party models, data, tools, plugins, and downstream integration.
